claims.claim: RELAI's talk frames continual learning as agents learning from feedback without forgetting.

support.reason: The speaker defines the goal of continual learning as agents learning from experience by acting, getting feedback, and improving without forgetting, which matches the claim.

claims.claim: Prime Intellect's talk covers an open-source post-training stack with asynchronous RL.

claims.claim: Microsoft's Ace talk argues voice agents need speed over frontier reasoning.

claims.claim: Superconductor's talk on multiplayer agentic engineering emphasizes shared sessions across interfaces.

claims.claim: Millennium argued centralized knowledge and thinner agents are key to organizational restructuring.

claims.claim: The Browser Company noted models execute well but still lack strong judgment.

claims.claim: Sierra expects most software pricing to move to outcome-based models as agents take on more autonomy.

claims.item: The agent supply chain (ungoverned skills, MCP servers)

claims.claim: A computer-use-agent evaluation talk shows a blind replay script (under a megabyte) matching or beating frontier models on standard benchmarks because the environments are deterministic.
claims.quote: the success rate of this agent compared to the uh frontier model from which the agent was extracted is actually uh the same or even better

claims.claim: The same talk proves pass@k on deterministic environments is formally equivalent to a replay agent's success rate, calling the metric itself gameable.

claims.claim: A talk titled 'A Genius With Amnesia' argues agents are constrained in both space (repo-bound) and time (no memory across sessions), forcing humans to become the memory.

support.reason: In context the speaker frames the problem as a space component (the agent is repo bound) and a time component (amnesia, where every session starts as a blank slate and the human becomes the memory), which matches the claim.

claims.claim: The same talk describes agents forced to re-explain the same intent repeatedly across repos due to lack of persistent memory, burning developer time and tokens.
claims.quote: Changing something across 20 repos means re-explaining things 20 times. A lot of developer time spent, but also a lot of tokens burned.

support.reason: The quote supports re-explaining the same change across 20 repos at a cost in developer time and tokens, but the speaker attributes this to agents being repo-bound (the "space" problem), not to the lack of persistent memory, which he treats as a separate second category.

claims.item: The harness carries reliability, not the model
claims.claim: Microsoft's Ace talk argues the model is talent and the harness is director; reliability is a control problem not a prompting problem.
claims.quote: The model is the talent, and the harness is the director... reliability was never a prompting problem. It's a control problem.

support.reason: The transcript has the speakers building Ace say both that reliability was never a prompting problem but a control problem, and that the model is the talent while the harness is the director.

claims.item: The harness carries reliability, not the model
claims.claim: Amazon's Mishra says the harness must catch the model's gaps so it fails gracefully.
claims.quote: harness has to detect all the gaps in the model and make it fail gracefully so that we are able to capture the failure modes

support.reason: The quote states directly that the harness has to detect the model's gaps and make it fail gracefully, which is exactly the claim.

claims.item: The harness carries reliability, not the model
claims.claim: Nearform credits harness engineering, not the model, for reliable autonomous coding.
claims.quote: Harness Engineering is the idea of building the environment around our coding agent so that they can work reliably

support.reason: The quote says harness engineering builds the environment that lets coding agents work reliably, but neither the quote nor its context contrasts this with the model or says reliability comes from the harness rather than the model.

claims.item: The harness carries reliability, not the model
claims.claim: Yutori argues scaffolding doesn't generalize; raw model capability over pixels does.
claims.quote: the more you end up writing scaffolds around existing websites the it doesn't actually generalize to the long tail of the web

support.reason: Calling it the bitter lesson for web agents, the speaker says scaffolds around existing websites don't generalize to the long tail of the web, and that the most general solution, 'just pixels in', is what generalizes.

claims.item: The harness carries reliability, not the model
claims.claim: Amazon's own talk also states the harness thins as the model improves.
claims.quote: over time, the model becomes better and better, and the harness becomes thinner and thinner

support.reason: The Amazon speaker says that early on the harness is strong and that over time, as the model becomes better, the harness becomes thinner, which matches the claim.

claims.item: The harness carries reliability, not the model
claims.claim: A continual-learning study found plain in-context learning beat elaborate context-management systems.

claims.item: The model is no longer the bottleneck
claims.claim: Composio argues the bottleneck moved from the model to the surrounding infrastructure.
claims.quote: For 2 years, the model was the bottleneck... Now, it's infrastructure that nobody has yet built

support.reason: In his closing takeaway the Composio speaker says the model was the bottleneck for two years, that the bottleneck has moved to infrastructure nobody has built yet, and that in future it will be the things around the model.

claims.item: The model is no longer the bottleneck
claims.claim: DeepMind's panel says video is a still-missing foundation model required for AGI.
claims.quote: It's a missing foundational model that's absolutely required if you want to make the AGI that match to humans

support.reason: In context, a panelist says their video model is more than pretty videos: it is a missing foundational model absolutely required to build human-matching AGI, which matches the claim.

claims.item: The model is no longer the bottleneck
claims.claim: Box's Ben Kus attributes the last year's agent capability leap to the model itself.
claims.quote: The big thing that changed last year was in my mind Opus 40 to Opus 45... the beginning the epic of like the new agent models

support.reason: Kus names the move from Opus 4.0 to Opus 4.5 as "the big thing that changed last year", saying it brought instruction following at high scale and began the era of new agent models, which attributes the leap to the model.

claims.item: Persistent memory is a first-class agent layer
claims.claim: A wearable-agent talk treats memory design as constitutive of the agent, with auto-raters for what to keep.
claims.quote: are these hierarchically related to each other or not... are we retrieving the right set of information given the current query

support.reason: The quote is from the list of auto-rater criteria (hierarchy, retrieval relevance), which supports the auto-rater part, but the idea that memory is constitutive of the agent comes from a separate earlier line ("the memory is what the agent becomes"), not from the cited quote.

claims.item: Persistent memory is a first-class agent layer
claims.claim: Sakana AI found memory added no capability, only cost, when the task already fit in context.
claims.quote: the memory actually didn't add more capability. It was the same performance with memory and without memory, and it only added more cost

support.reason: The speaker says that because all papers fit in context, memory gave the same performance as no memory and only added cost, which is what the claim states.

claims.item: Persistent memory is a first-class agent layer
claims.claim: A memory-systems survey argues memory cannot be a generic outsourced layer, contrary to memory-as-a-product framing.
claims.quote: memory cannot be outsourced. If you're a serious team, you do not outsource memory. It is something that you build alongside your product

support.reason: The speaker, drawing on his study of memory systems, says there is no single way to do memory, so serious teams should not outsource it but build it in-house with their product, which clearly implies rejecting memory as an outsourced product layer.

items.label: The Model Is Not the Bottleneck

claims.claim: Microsoft's Ace argues reliability is a harness/control problem, not a model problem
claims.quote: It proposes, but ultimately it is the harness that decides.

support.reason: In context, the speakers say the harness decides rather than the model, and that a smaller model performs reliably because of the harnessing, so if reliability is a coin flip you should take control flow out of the model; this clearly frames reliability as a harness/control issue rather than a model one.

claims.claim: Anthropic frames the harness as now the limiting factor on model capability
claims.quote: harnesses have become the limiting factor to what models can achieve

support.reason: The Anthropic speaker states directly that as models evolve, harnesses have become the limiting factor to what models can achieve, which matches the claim.

claims.claim: Yutori argues scaffolding around the web doesn't generalize the way raw model capability does
claims.quote: the more you end up writing scaffolds around existing websites the it doesn't actually generalize to the long tail of the web

support.reason: Framing it as the 'bitter lesson' for web agents, the speaker says scaffolds around existing websites don't generalize to the long tail of the web, while the general solution (a vision model taking pixels in) does, which matches the claim's contrast.

claims.claim: Anthropic's own talk shows harness fixes become dead weight as the model improves
claims.quote: the harness fixes were no longer needed and were actually detracting from model performance with Opus 4.5

support.reason: The Anthropic speakers explain that context-reset fixes added to the harness for Sonnet 4.5 became "dead weight" once Opus 4.5 arrived and in fact hurt performance, which states the claim directly.

claims.claim: Amazon frames the harness as shrinking, not growing, as the model matures
claims.quote: the model becomes better and better, and the harness becomes thinner and thinner

support.reason: The Amazon AGI Lab speaker says the harness is strong early on and that over time, as the model becomes better and better, the harness becomes thinner and thinner, which is the shrinking framing the claim describes.

claims.item: The Model Is Not the Bottleneck
claims.claim: Veric argues execution/intelligence is solved and business understanding is the real bottleneck
claims.quote: clearly execution is no longer the core bottleneck... intelligence is no longer the constraint

support.reason: The speaker says execution is no longer the core bottleneck and intelligence is no longer the constraint, then names understanding the business as the remaining bottleneck.

claims.item: The Model Is Not the Bottleneck
claims.claim: A solo founder argues implementation is solved and judgment/taste is the remaining bottleneck
claims.quote: implementation is mostly solved... the thing that doesn't work is our judgment and our taste

support.reason: The speaker says he built the product alone and is "still alone with some support," then states that implementation is mostly solved while judgment and taste are what don't work, which matches the claim.

claims.item: The Model Is Not the Bottleneck
claims.claim: SWE-Marathon shows even the best agent/model configuration is far from solving project-scale work
claims.quote: the best configuration here is Claude Opus 4.8 with Claude Code, and it only achieves a 26% resolution rate

support.reason: The quote gives the best configuration's 26% resolution rate, and the context adds that even the strongest setup solves only about one in four tasks and that end-to-end project ownership is still very far from solved.

claims.item: The Model Is Not the Bottleneck
claims.claim: CUA's GUI benchmark shows agents still fail most professional tasks, especially from a blank start
claims.quote: the top agent that we tested only got a full pass on six out of 25 of these tasks

support.reason: The quote and its context say the top agent fully passed only 6 of 25 professional electrical-engineering tasks, all of them edits to existing schematics, and that success dropped to 0% from a blank schematic, which matches the claim.

claims.claim: A memory-systems survey finds ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini's architectures converged on a running profile
claims.quote: while the general architectures have converged, the spec specific implementation details are still very different

support.reason: The context says ChatGPT and Claude converged on a running profile, that general architectures have converged, and that Gemini also has a running profile, though the speaker adds that implementation details still differ.

claims.claim: A wearable-agent talk argues memory now defines what the agent is
claims.quote: The memory is what the agent becomes and it's becoming in real time it's evolving in real time

support.reason: In context the speaker contrasts the model as "just the engine" with memory as "what the agent becomes", which amounts to saying memory defines the agent, and the title line establishes this is a wearable-agent talk.

claims.claim: The same memory-systems speaker argues memory cannot be outsourced as a product
claims.quote: memory cannot be outsourced. If you're a serious team, you do not outsource memory

support.reason: The speaker states that memory cannot be outsourced, that serious teams should build it alongside their product, and notes that top consumer products all build memory in-house rather than outsourcing it.

claims.claim: Sakana's research found memory adds no benefit and only cost when the task fits in context
claims.quote: the memory actually didn't add more capability. It was the same performance with memory and without memory, and it only added more cost

support.reason: The speaker, from Sakana AI, reports that on the literature-review task, where everything fit in context, memory gave the same performance as no memory and only added cost, which is exactly what the claim says.

claims.claim: Netflix built fleet-wide agent memory as plain markdown in Git rather than a sophisticated memory product
claims.quote: not very fancy vector search or or a vector database... you can start with just a markdown files in a in a centralized Git repo

support.reason: The speaker says the fleet-wide memory needn't be a fancy vector database and that 'you can start with' markdown files in a central Git repo, but he frames this as a recommendation rather than stating that Netflix actually built it this way.
